taxonomy.title: Stomach — ulcer, bleeding and emptying disorders
taxonomy.scopeIn: Peptic ulcer, H. pylori, nonvariceal upper GI bleeding, gastric outlet obstruction, gastroparesis and post-gastrectomy benign physiology.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Gastric tumors belong to stomach-neoplasia. Bariatric-anatomy complications belong to bariatric-metabolic. Portal hypertensive bleeding belongs to liver-benign-portal-infection.
taxonomy.priorityReason: Bleeding and obstruction offer central diagnosis, intervention and rescue decisions.

records.title: Sequence treatment of recurrent ulcer bleeding
fairness: The explicit 'no repeat ... yet' hint is gone. The resident must distinguish recurrence after successful initial hemostasis from persistent failure, then choose the next therapeutic stage in a resuscitated patient with an accessible target.

Repeat therapeutic endoscopy is the defensible best offered plan. Angiographic and operative rescue remain clinically credible alternatives, and access/availability information is necessary for ranking them rather than an expendable cue.

Moderate two-step application. The 118/72 pressure and pulse 94 are case observations, not taught cutoffs. The local ledger maps the rebleeding sequence to its retained ESGE source; this offline review cannot authenticate the cited external guideline or correction history. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain successful-first-treatment chronology, current response, target access and equal availability. Do not add the named-missing-repeat sentence back.

records.title: Structural assessment before gastric emptying
fairness: The interrupted examination and prepyloric-only histology leave an irregular pyloric narrowing unevaluated. Interpreting that sampling limitation and prioritizing targeted endoscopy over a motility study is a consequential two-step decision. Contrast passage does not by itself establish that the structural lesion is irrelevant.

Importance: high-yield differentiation of structural obstruction from diabetic dysmotility. Realism: decompression before re-evaluation is plausible. Repeat endoscopy needs an appropriate aspiration-risk/anesthetic plan, but absence of its technical details does not make the offered diagnostic ranking unfair.
suggestions: Preserve the exact site and adequacy distinctions; do not replace the raw record with 'inconclusive endoscopy' or a diagnosed obstruction label.

records.title: Antibody results after a valid eradication test
fairness: The medication timeline must be reconciled across the later antibiotic, PPI and bismuth exposures, then translated into the earliest applicable collection date. Fourteen days is a credible near-miss if the resident accounts for PPI and antibiotics but misses bismuth.
Using the usual washout framework intended by the item, the latest constraint is 21 days from today. The answer is a calendar consequence, not a universal new duration invented for this patient.

Importance: high for valid eradication testing. Realism: clinic follow-up and medication-calendar review are plausible. The antibiotic identity/indication is broad but does not create a better offered date on the intended general interference rule.

The positive antibody and prior negative on-PPI sample are background because the clinician has already selected repeat stool testing; they should not be counted as an additional scored diagnostic inference.
suggestions: Retain the competing washout dates and have the clinician verify the exact test/preparation rules.
Shorten the already resolved antibody discussion if it has no role in the displayed sequence; do not claim this item independently tests both serology interpretation and test timing.

records.title: Recurrent ulcer bleeding

cues.phrase: The previous clip arms have caught thin superficial edges that are separating from the base.
cues.why: A nonmedical reader can use failed-tool repetition to discount another through-the-scope clip. However, this does not distinguish deeper endoscopic capture from arterial embolization; the observation is necessary failure-mechanism evidence, not a sufficient answer shortcut.

fairness: Node node.n4.ulcer-recurrent-bleeding-after-clips.v2: infer inadequate superficial purchase rather than simply an untreated second vessel, then decide whether the accessible focal target supports a different capture strategy before ending endoscopic treatment. Repeating the prior tool and escalating immediately are recognizable competing errors.

A cap-mounted clip is the defensible best of the three offered strategies for this stabilized patient with recurrent focal bleeding and a stable frontal view. The view and tissue-response observations support considering additional endoscopic treatment, but do not guarantee successful capture or hemostasis.

The prior device-specific permission sentence has been replaced by observations. The options are concrete and similarly scoped; the task no longer grammatically excludes embolization. No convergence, diagnosis-label giveaway or uniquely qualified key is apparent.

Phase genuinely fits: the bleeding point and prior clip behavior are being observed during repeat endoscopy. The embolization choice explicitly ends this attempt, so it is a current escalation decision rather than a claim that embolization occurs through the endoscope.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Exact device suitability remains a clinician judgment; the item does not establish that another conventional clip could never work or that embolization is never appropriate.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between superficial clip purchase and the current focal access rather than reducing the item to recurrent bleeding followed by a device name.
Keep escalation phrased as the decision to end the current attempt. Do not convert the tissue observations into an assurance that the lesion can be drawn into the keyed device.

value.patientPresentation: An adult with diabetes has chronic nausea, early satiety, postprandial fullness, and vomiting. Imaging has excluded mechanical obstruction.
value.stem: Which study should be used to confirm delayed gastric emptying?

answerChoices.label: Upper gastrointestinal contrast study with small-bowel follow-through
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A contrast study may evaluate anatomy and transit patterns but is not the approved standardized test for documenting solid-meal gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Prolonged ambulatory reflux monitoring off acid suppression
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Reflux monitoring measures esophageal reflux exposure and does not confirm delayed gastric emptying.

answerChoices.label: Four-hour scintigraphy after a standardized solid meal
High-resolution esophageal manometry with impedance monitoring
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Esophageal manometry evaluates esophageal motor function rather than gastric emptying.

value.explanation: Once mechanical obstruction has been excluded, a four-hour standardized solid-meal scintigraphic study provides objective evidence of delayed gastric emptying.

value.stem: Which diagnostic plan should the hospital use next for {patientName}'s vomiting?
value.explanation: Retained food in diabetes does not establish gastroparesis. The first examination was preparation-limited; decompression and persistent contrast passage support a prepared repeat examination rather than treating prior termination as proof that endoscopic access is impossible. Assess and sample the irregular pyloric lesion before moving to emptying physiology. This is a diagnostic plan, not an instruction to force a scope through a tight obstruction.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: CT after decompression
items.value: Short irregular mural thickening at the pyloric channel with a narrowed lumen; oral contrast passes into the duodenum

items.label: Nasogastric course
items.value: Food residue initially returned; drainage subsequently became clear and diminished

items.label: Current condition
items.value: Blood pressure maintained, abdomen soft; liquids had passed before admission

answerChoices.label: Repeat endoscopy with pyloric biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: The first procedure ended because of retained contents, not an impassable proven stricture. Decompression changes the acquisition conditions, and the irregular structural lesion warrants direct assessment and tissue.

answerChoices.label: Contrast fluoroscopy with pyloric transit mapping
answerChoices.rationale: Fluoroscopy can characterize transit, but contrast already passes and it would not characterize the irregular mural lesion histologically.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Fluoroscopy can characterize transit, but contrast already passes and it would not characterize the irregular mural lesion histologically.

answerChoices.label: Prepared four-hour gastric-emptying scintigraphy
answerChoices.rationale: This is the appropriate physiology protocol after structural exclusion; diabetes and retained food do not supply that prerequisite.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is the appropriate physiology protocol after structural exclusion; diabetes and retained food do not supply that prerequisite.

value.displayName: Structural assessment before gastric emptying
value.presentation: {patientName}, a 65-year-old man with diabetes, attends clinic with vomiting and early satiety. His outside gastroscopy was stopped when retained food regurgitated during sedation. The mucosal specimen obtained before that event showed inflamed prepyloric mucosa. He was admitted for hydration and gastric decompression; the subsequent record is shown below.

value.stem: Which collection date should be used for {patientName}'s planned stool antigen test if these medicines remain stopped?
value.explanation: The old negative active test was obtained during PPI exposure, while a positive antibody result does not supply a prepared active-infection cure test. Use the complete subsequent medication record. The recorded plan requires two weeks off PPI and four weeks off antibiotics or bismuth. At day 21 from today, all three holds are satisfied; at day 14 the bismuth hold is not. These are source-supported clinical preparation intervals, not authored laboratory turnaround times.

value.stem: Which hemostatic strategy should be selected next for {patientName}?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed clinical record; fictional observations

items.label: Current endoscopic field
items.value: A discrete point between the prior clips is spurting. The ulcer lies on a broad fibrotic base facing the endoscope; the lumen permits a stable frontal view.

items.label: Tissue response
items.value: The previous clip arms have caught thin superficial edges that are separating from the base. Gentle contact around the bleeding point indents the surrounding tissue without uncovering a deep cavity.

answerChoices.label: Place a cap-mounted clip across the focal vessel
answerChoices.rationale: This is recurrent focal bleeding after initial conventional hemostasis, with poor superficial purchase. Cap-mounted clipping offers a repeat endoscopic approach before declaring repeat therapy unsuccessful.

answerChoices.label: Place a through-the-scope hemostatic clip at the vessel
answerChoices.rationale: The separating superficial edges make repeating the same type of purchase less persuasive in this recurrent setting.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The separating superficial edges make repeating the same type of purchase less persuasive in this recurrent setting.

answerChoices.label: End this attempt and proceed to arterial embolization
answerChoices.rationale: Repeat endoscopic treatment has not yet failed in the stabilized patient with a visible target. Embolization is the escalation when repeat therapy fails or is infeasible.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeat endoscopic treatment has not yet failed in the stabilized patient with a visible target. Embolization is the escalation when repeat therapy fails or is infeasible.

value.explanation: Distinguish recurrence after initial success from failure of repeat endoscopic treatment. Use the focal target and superficial clip-edge separation to reconsider tissue capture. Cap-mounted clipping is the best offered repeat approach. Another superficial clip repeats the observed purchase problem; embolization remains the escalation if repeat endoscopic treatment fails.

value.patientPresentation: During hospital EGD for an actively oozing ulcer, the team compares conventional plans that use epinephrine for initial temporary control with plans that provide definitive hemostasis.
value.stem: Which plan fails to provide a definitive second modality after epinephrine?

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine followed by bipolar coagulation of the identified vessel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Bipolar coagulation supplies the definitive contact-thermal modality after epinephrine.

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine followed by endoscopic clipping of the identified vessel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Clipping supplies the definitive mechanical modality after epinephrine.

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine followed only by another epinephrine injection
Bipolar coagulation without injection therapy to definitively treat the vessel
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This uses a definitive thermal modality rather than relying on epinephrine monotherapy; the question does not claim injection is mandatory in every accepted pathway.

value.explanation: When the conventional epinephrine pathway is selected for active ulcer bleeding, temporary injection control must be followed by definitive thermal or mechanical hemostasis. This does not make every noninjection monotherapy universally wrong; selected advanced alternatives belong to a separate expert pathway.

value.patientPresentation: A resuscitated hospitalized adult has an actively bleeding peptic ulcer at EGD. The endoscopist elects to use the conventional epinephrine-combination pathway with mechanical hemostasis.
value.stem: Which complete treatment plan follows that pathway?

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine injection alone
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Epinephrine alone lacks the definitive mechanical modality specified by the chosen pathway.

answerChoices.label: Epinephrine plus saline injection without definitive hemostasis
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A second injection without a definitive thermal or mechanical modality does not complete the pathway.

answerChoices.label: Repeated epinephrine injections without definitive therapy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating epinephrine does not substitute for definitive mechanical or thermal hemostasis.

value.patientPresentation: A resuscitated hospitalized adult has an actively oozing duodenal ulcer during EGD. Dilute epinephrine is injected and the bleeding slows.
value.stem: What should the endoscopist do next?

answerChoices.label: Apply bipolar coagulation to the vessel
End the procedure because the bleeding slowed
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Temporary slowing after epinephrine does not provide definitive hemostasis.

answerChoices.label: Inject additional epinephrine and then stop
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Additional epinephrine still leaves the ulcer without a definitive second modality.

answerChoices.label: Observe the vessel without definitive treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Observation does not complete hemostasis after temporary injection control of active bleeding.

value.explanation: When the conventional epinephrine pathway is selected for active ulcer bleeding, temporary injection control must be followed by definitive thermal or mechanical hemostasis. value.patientPresentation: A hospitalized adult with melena has been resuscitated and undergoes EGD. A duodenal ulcer is actively oozing blood.
value.stem: What is the appropriate endoscopic response?

answerChoices.label: Observe because the bleeding appears venous
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Active oozing from a peptic ulcer is a treatment indication regardless of this unsupported characterization.

answerChoices.label: Use oral PPI alone and end the procedure
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Medication alone does not replace endoscopic hemostasis for an actively bleeding ulcer.

answerChoices.label: Delay treatment until a second bleeding episode
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The present active bleed is already an indication for endoscopic hemostasis.

value.stem: Which hemostasis plan should be arranged next for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Repeat therapeutic upper endoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Clinical recurrent bleeding after an initially successful course supports another endoscopic attempt, with a cap-mounted clip considered for recurrence.

answerChoices.label: Transcatheter arterial embolization
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This bypasses the usual second endoscopic attempt in the resuscitated patient with an accessible target and no documented repeat failure.

answerChoices.label: Operative ulcer hemostasis
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Primary surgery bypasses less invasive repeat endoscopy and angiographic options available in this setting.

value.stem: How should {patientName}'s later antibody result affect the eradication decision?

answerChoices.label: Retain the valid active-infection test-of-cure conclusion
answerChoices.rationale: Serology is not the active-infection test used to establish eradication; it does not overturn the properly prepared stool result in this record.

answerChoices.label: Repeat eradication treatment from the positive antibody result
answerChoices.rationale: This uses antibody evidence as though it demonstrated current infection despite the valid active-infection assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This uses antibody evidence as though it demonstrated current infection despite the valid active-infection assessment.

answerChoices.label: Use serial antibody results to decide whether treatment worked
answerChoices.rationale: The supported cure pathway uses a breath or stool active-infection test with appropriate preparation, not serial serology.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The supported cure pathway uses a breath or stool active-infection test with appropriate preparation, not serial serology.

value.explanation: The supported eradication assessment is an active-infection test after the required medication washout. That preparation is documented. A later positive antibody result is not proof of persistent active infection and should not automatically trigger another eradication course.

answerChoices.rationale: The injection response is temporary control rather than the definitive companion modality, and the ulcer still requires appropriate PPI treatment afterward.

answerChoices.rationale: This completes the endoscopic component but replaces the supported post-hemostasis PPI component.

value.stem: Which next hemostatic procedure best fits {patientName}'s later change?
value.explanation: The isolated early dark stool does not establish the same event as later fresh hematemesis with a new hemoglobin fall and hypotension. The later sequence supports recurrent bleeding after completed initial hemostasis. Repeat therapeutic endoscopy is the best offered next procedure; embolization and surgery are important rescue paths when suitable endoscopic treatment fails or the clinical situation changes. Acid suppression and resuscitation remain shared care. This does not assert that clipping is superior to every other endoscopic method.

value.stem: Which treatment should the endoscopist apply next to {patientName}'s ulcer?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Before injection
items.value: A stream of red blood emerges from one point in the ulcer base.

items.label: After dilute epinephrine injection
items.value: The stream stops. Irrigation exposes a raised red point at the same site; it remains raised when the surrounding clot washes away.

answerChoices.label: Mechanical clipping at the bleeding point
answerChoices.rationale: The injection response does not complete treatment of this remaining high-risk point; mechanical hemostasis supplies a definitive modality.

answerChoices.label: Repeat epinephrine injection at the point
answerChoices.rationale: More injection without a definitive modality repeats temporary treatment rather than completing vessel therapy.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: More injection without a definitive modality repeats temporary treatment rather than completing vessel therapy.

answerChoices.label: Topical hemostatic powder over the point
answerChoices.rationale: Topical powder is not routine sole initial definitive treatment of this exposed vessel when a standard definitive modality is feasible.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Topical powder is not routine sole initial definitive treatment of this exposed vessel when a standard definitive modality is feasible.

value.explanation: Stopping the stream after injection is not the same as completing definitive ulcer hemostasis. The persistent raised point is a vessel stigma requiring local treatment. Apply mechanical hemostasis here; repeating epinephrine does not replace a definitive thermal or mechanical modality. This does not make every form of advanced monotherapy inappropriate.

singleBest.key: Urea breath testing after PPI washout

authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the on-PPI collection condition and the premise for repeat active testing changes. Alarm negatives retain their job of ranking invasive reassessment.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If vomiting and a new irregular outlet lesion accompanied the unresolved tests, upper endoscopy with biopsy would become the priority.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: The subsequent node receives a later positive prepared test. This feedback teaches assay validity, not the later antibiotic regimen.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: No assertion that breath testing is superior to a properly prepared stool antigen test; that equally valid alternative is not offered.

caseDefinition.learningSummary: A correctly prepared active-infection test has a different role from antibody serology. Preserve the supported cure assessment rather than prescribe another course for IgG positivity.

statementMapping.constructedObservationBasis: Original fictional named patients, dates, drug-exposure histories, acquired findings, operation records and actual response trajectories. Measurements are observations, not new epidemiologic weights, probabilities or clinical cutoffs.
statementMapping.numericRuleBasis: Any patient numbers are constructed observations. Four-hour acquisition and the 14-day BQT course are directly supported protocol/treatment facts, not operational waits.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: Replaced abstract retain-the-conclusion wording with actual prescribing plans. No generic individualized key. The symptom resolution is supportive context, not proof of eradication; medication and assay identity determine the answer.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three current antibiotic-prescribing decisions.

reasoning.interpret: Check every relevant medication interval before accepting the negative active assay, then distinguish antibody persistence from current infection.
reasoning.apply: Avoid an unnecessary eradication course.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Moderate predicted: the trap is privileging a newer positive assay over a properly prepared active test.

singleBest.key: Do not prescribe another eradication course
singleBest.decidingObservation: The earlier active test is negative with adequate preparation; the later positive test is antibody-based.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Unnecessary antibiotics create adverse effects and avoidable selection pressure.

authorGate.deletionTest: Without preparation data, the negative test cannot carry this conclusion and re-evaluation would be needed.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: A positive prepared active assay after prior clarithromycin failure, with no prior BQT, would support BQT.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Standalone; no prior calendar question teaches that this particular specimen was valid.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: Clinical review must confirm the assay/preparation assumptions. No claim that symptoms alone demonstrate cure.

competitorAudit.temptation: Treat the latest positive laboratory label as the decisive result.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: BQT treats established infection; IgG positivity does not establish persistence after this adequately prepared negative active test.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: A prepared active-infection test is positive and prior-regimen history supports BQT.

competitorAudit.temptation: Assume a positive follow-up antibody requires a different antibiotic family.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: Neither persistent infection nor levofloxacin susceptibility is demonstrated by antibody positivity.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Persistent active infection and susceptibility-guided salvage support that regimen.

decisionNodes.stem: Which longer-term nutrition route best fits {patientName}'s observed feeding response?

answerChoices.label: Jejunal enteral feeding access
answerChoices.rationale: The trial demonstrates that bypassing the stomach can deliver the prescribed nutrition. It supports an enteral route beyond the dysfunctional stomach.

answerChoices.label: Gastric enteral feeding access
answerChoices.rationale: This places the feed in the compartment that repeatedly regurgitated it; permanent access does not itself correct that observed tolerance problem.

answerChoices.label: Central venous parenteral nutrition
answerChoices.rationale: The record demonstrates a usable enteral route. Parenteral nutrition is not required simply because gastric emptying is severely impaired.

statementMapping.constructedObservationBasis: Original fictional named patients, dates, drug-exposure histories, acquired findings, operation records and actual response trajectories. Measurements are observations, not new epidemiologic weights, probabilities or clinical cutoffs.
statementMapping.numericRuleBasis: Any patient numbers are constructed observations. Four-hour acquisition and the 14-day BQT course are directly supported protocol/treatment facts, not operational waits.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: The old result-label question was replaced by an acquisition decision. The task does not say confirm gastroparesis. All choices are named investigations with waits. Necessary adequacy observations are retained without the sentence no repeat test yet.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Diagnostic investigations after persistent symptoms and review of actual prior acquisition.

reasoning.interpret: The outlet was examined adequately, but the normal two-hour result does not establish the later emptying result.
reasoning.apply: Choose the investigation that fills the remaining physiologic evidence gap.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Moderate predicted: distinguish a normal early observation from a complete negative study and keep structural versus motility workup separate.

singleBest.key: Solid-meal scintigraphy with four-hour acquisition
singleBest.decidingObservation: The acquisition log ends at two hours while the outlet examination is complete.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Prematurely closing the emptying question can mislabel persistent symptoms or trigger inappropriate treatment.

authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the acquisition log makes the word normal misleadingly conclusive; deleting the outlet details leaves repeat endoscopy reasonable.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If the endoscope had stopped before an irregular pyloric lesion and sampled only proximal mucosa, repeat targeted endoscopy would take priority.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Feedback discusses acquisition only. The next node receives a later completed test and asks a nutrition decision, not the same test choice.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: Clinical review of symptom plausibility and esophageal distractor required; no test-sensitivity percentage or new threshold is authored.

competitorAudit.temptation: Treat persistent vomiting as proof the structural examination must have missed the cause.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: An adequate recent examination already addressed an outlet lesion. Repeating that structural assessment does not supply the missing emptying acquisition.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: A new focal outlet abnormality or an incomplete earlier examination reopens the structural question.

competitorAudit.temptation: Substitute another motility test for the gastric measurement.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: The unresolved evidence concerns gastric emptying rather than esophageal propulsion or passage at the esophagogastric junction.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Swallow-related dysphagia or regurgitation with an esophageal motor question remains after structural evaluation.

caseDefinition.learningSummary: Separate an adequate outlet examination from an incomplete emptying acquisition. A two-hour report cannot supply an unacquired four-hour measurement. Use a standardized solid-meal protocol with direct later imaging. Dietary treatment must fit both the emptying disorder and actual food tolerance. Use small, lower-fat and lower-fiber meals, with blended foods as needed, before concluding that oral nutrition has failed. The decisive evidence is successful delivery and retention during the postpyloric trial after oral and gastric routes failed. Consider jejunal access; parenteral nutrition remains a fallback when adequate enteral support cannot be delivered.

statementMapping.constructedObservationBasis: Original fictional named patients, dates, drug-exposure histories, acquired findings, operation records and actual response trajectories. Measurements are observations, not new epidemiologic weights, probabilities or clinical cutoffs.
statementMapping.numericRuleBasis: Any patient numbers are constructed observations. Four-hour acquisition and the 14-day BQT course are directly supported protocol/treatment facts, not operational waits.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: All options are small-meal prescriptions of similar scope; no uniquely comprehensive feeding-access key. The task does not say low residue. The known diagnosis is appropriate because the scored task is treatment.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three oral dietary prescriptions before oral nutrition has been optimized.

reasoning.interpret: Whole solids are poorly retained while blended intake remains possible; a standard high-fiber diet is not serving this new physiology.
reasoning.apply: Select a gastric-tolerance nutrition plan rather than maximize fiber or solid calorie density.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Moderate predicted, with a residual risk of being too familiar for PGY-2/3; independent review must assess the fiber-versus-gastric-tolerance error.

singleBest.key: Small low-fat, low-fiber meals with blended foods
singleBest.decidingObservation: Retained recognizable solids and successful blended intake occur with documented delayed solid emptying.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: An ill-matched diet can perpetuate vomiting and inadequate nutrition.

authorGate.deletionTest: Without the diet log and food-form response, the item becomes simple dietary recall; those observations defeat the credible generic diabetes-diet error.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If delayed emptying were not present and the actual dietary problem were fiber-responsive bowel symptoms with preserved food tolerance, the whole-grain/bran plan could become reasonable.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Prior feedback establishes test adequacy, not diet composition. This feedback does not name the next node's feeding route.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: Government diet guidance is broad; calorie, fluid and diabetes medication adjustments remain outside the keyed objective.

competitorAudit.temptation: Continue a usual diabetes-oriented high-fiber strategy despite the changed gastric problem.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: Generic high-fiber advice does not address the retained rough solids that now limit this patient's intake.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: An appropriate dietary problem calls for more fiber and the patient tolerates it; this is not the current gastric plan.

competitorAudit.temptation: Treat the nutritional risk by increasing calorie density without considering gastric processing.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: Concentrating solid calories with fat does not match the low-fat, easier-to-process dietary approach or her observed food tolerance.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: A different nutrition problem and demonstrated fat tolerance justify that prescription; no such evidence is given here.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: All labels are concrete feeding routes. No generic individualized plan or uniquely complete key. Successful trial language is essential response evidence, not permission that an untested procedure is feasible.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three longer-term nutrition-access strategies after demonstrated treatment responses.

reasoning.interpret: The stomach has failed as a feeding reservoir, but the intestinal trial demonstrates adequate enteral delivery.
reasoning.apply: Choose durable jejunal rather than gastric or intravenous feeding.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Moderate predicted: distinguish gastric failure from intestinal failure using what nutrition was actually delivered.

singleBest.key: Jejunal enteral feeding access
singleBest.decidingObservation: The prescribed postpyloric feed was actually delivered and retained, not merely planned.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Ignoring the response can cause recurrent gastric-feed failure or avoidable central-line nutrition exposure.

authorGate.deletionTest: Remove actual trial delivery/tolerance and the long-term route is insufficiently established; a proposed trial would not prove success.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If appropriately placed postpyloric feeding repeatedly failed to provide nutrition and enteral delivery could not be achieved, parenteral nutrition would become reasonable.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Diet feedback did not name jejunal or parenteral routes. The later admission supplies new consequential response data; no future findings were used earlier.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: Single adequate government source; access technique and exact nutrition targets require clinician selection and are not tested.

competitorAudit.temptation: Choose the simpler common feeding tube without using the trial response.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: This places the feed in the compartment that repeatedly regurgitated it; permanent access does not itself correct that observed tolerance problem.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: The stomach can retain adequate feeds and the primary limitation is safe oral delivery.

competitorAudit.temptation: Equate failure of oral and gastric feeding with failure of the whole intestinal route.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: The record demonstrates a usable enteral route. Parenteral nutrition is not required simply because gastric emptying is severely impaired.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Adequate postpyloric nutrition cannot be achieved or enteral feeding is contraindicated.

Use controlled preparation rather than a universal drug-hold or glucose cutoff invented for the case.

reasoning.interpret: The test measured emptying during opioid exposure and excess glucose; the subsequent improvement is evidence against treating that result as a fixed current phenotype.
reasoning.apply: Obtain an interpretable current emptying measurement before a pylorus-specific selection test.

singleBest.consequenceOfError: Premature invasive treatment can target a reversible or no-longer-present abnormality.

authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the medication/glucose record and interval improvement turns repeat testing into an unsupported delay. The four-hour acquisition must remain to distinguish this from the short-study item.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If repeated properly prepared studies showed continuing delay despite optimized medical care, a pyloric distensibility assessment could become reasonable during specialist procedural evaluation.

statementMapping.constructedObservationBasis: Original fictional named patients, dates, drug-exposure histories, acquired findings, operation records and actual response trajectories. Measurements are observations, not new epidemiologic weights, probabilities or clinical cutoffs.
statementMapping.numericRuleBasis: Any patient numbers are constructed observations. Four-hour acquisition and the 14-day BQT course are directly supported protocol/treatment facts, not operational waits.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: Every site has an observation; all options name the same action at one site and use parallel lengths. No protected image is promised. The prose record is the actual exhibit; a diagnosis label is withheld without withholding necessary geometry.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three site-specific local-hemostasis actions during the same endoscopy.

reasoning.interpret: Distinguish the raised nonbleeding focus from two low-risk base appearances.
reasoning.apply: Localize the consequential hemostatic action to the correct site.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Moderate predicted; tests record interpretation and wrong-site risk rather than an abstract high-risk label. Residual recognition simplicity is flagged for independent review.

singleBest.key: Place hemostatic clips at the duodenal-bulb focus
singleBest.decidingObservation: A projection persists above the duodenal floor; the gastric dark mark is level with its floor.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Treating the wrong site leaves the high-risk vessel untreated while exposing another lesion to an unnecessary procedure.

authorGate.deletionTest: Without the level-versus-raised observations, color and anatomical labels cannot establish the best target.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Swap the body and duodenal geometric observations, keeping the labels and dry field unchanged, and the gastric-body treatment becomes correct.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Standalone to prevent earlier feedback classifying a companion lesion or rehearsing the same geometry.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: Clinical review must confirm the prose observations distinguish a vessel; no device-specific superiority is asserted.

competitorAudit.temptation: Treat a dark mark as evidence requiring local treatment regardless of its geometry.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: The body finding is flat after lavage. Its dark color does not give it the same significance as a protruding vessel.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: That site instead has active bleeding or a protruding vessel.

competitorAudit.temptation: Treat the visible crater with the most extensive surface material.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: A fibrin-covered even base without a vessel or flow is not the high-risk target described in this record.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: That site instead shows active bleeding or a protruding vessel after appropriate inspection.

statementMapping.constructedObservationBasis: Original fictional named patients, dates, drug-exposure histories, acquired findings, operation records and actual response trajectories. Measurements are observations, not new epidemiologic weights, probabilities or clinical cutoffs.
statementMapping.numericRuleBasis: ESGE directly supports a 72-hour initial high-dose PPI phase. One elapsed day is a constructed chronology.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: Three medication courses have parallel labels. The history does not announce that PPI was omitted. A known treated lesion is needed for the regimen task; current absence of bleeding is necessary response evidence, not a safety giveaway.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Three acid-suppression courses at a defined post-hemostasis stage.

reasoning.interpret: The later dry base documents treatment response, not low-risk pretreatment stigmata.
reasoning.apply: Retain the initial post-hemostasis PPI course before moving to ulcer-healing intensity.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Moderate predicted: distinguish pretreatment risk from observed treatment response and course completion.

singleBest.key: Continue the initial high-dose pantoprazole course
singleBest.decidingObservation: Spurting required successful hemostasis and only one day of the initial course has elapsed.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Mistaking response for original risk can prematurely discontinue a supported protective treatment phase.

authorGate.deletionTest: Remove either the original spurting/hemostasis record or the elapsed course stage and the current dry view cannot establish the required intensity.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: After completion of the initial high-dose course, a clinically appropriate oral ulcer-healing course becomes reasonable.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Standalone; the low-risk case is not a preceding scored companion. No feedback reveals another item's regimen.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: No claim that pantoprazole is uniquely superior to another accepted high-dose PPI or that the later EGD is routine care.

competitorAudit.temptation: Treat a later dry view as though the index ulcer had always been low risk.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: That is an appropriate later stage but downstages the represented initial post-hemostasis phase prematurely.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: The initial high-dose course is complete or the index lesion had low-risk stigmata without hemostasis.

competitorAudit.temptation: Assume procedural success makes acid-suppression intensity or class unimportant.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: A dry endoscopic field does not replace the supported post-hemostasis PPI indication with an H2-based strategy.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: A separately justified non-PPI acid strategy is needed; no such constraint appears in this record.

value.stem: Which next hemostatic procedure best fits {patientName}'s later change?
value.explanation: The isolated early dark stool does not establish the same event as later fresh hematemesis with a new hemoglobin fall and hypotension. The later sequence supports recurrent bleeding after completed initial hemostasis. Repeat therapeutic endoscopy is the best offered next procedure; embolization and surgery are important rescue paths when suitable endoscopic treatment fails or the clinical situation changes. Acid suppression and resuscitation remain shared care. This does not assert that clipping is superior to every other endoscopic method.

One dark stool; hemoglobin 9.1 then 9.0 g/dL; no fresh emesis
Fresh red hematemesis with a new fall in hemoglobin to 7.6 g/dL and transient hypotension
Alert; blood pressure 118/70 mmHg; abdomen soft

value.learningSummary: The isolated early dark stool does not establish the same event as later fresh hematemesis with a new hemoglobin fall and hypotension. The later sequence supports recurrent bleeding after completed initial hemostasis. Repeat therapeutic endoscopy is the best offered next procedure; embolization and surgery are important rescue paths when suitable endoscopic treatment fails or the clinical situation changes. Acid suppression and resuscitation remain shared care. This does not assert that clipping is superior to every other endoscopic method.

statementMapping.constructedObservationBasis: Original fictional named patients, dates, drug-exposure histories, acquired findings, operation records and actual response trajectories. Measurements are observations, not new epidemiologic weights, probabilities or clinical cutoffs.
statementMapping.numericRuleBasis: Any patient numbers are constructed observations. Four-hour acquisition and the 14-day BQT course are directly supported protocol/treatment facts, not operational waits.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: Removed named missing-action and equal-availability permission sentences. Every option is a concrete hemostatic procedure with a preview estimate. No future failure is disclosed in the current context or feedback.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Hemostatic procedure selection after recurrence and resuscitation.

reasoning.interpret: Separate old blood passage without a new trend from the later episode with fresh emesis and a new circulatory/hemoglobin change.
reasoning.apply: Use present resuscitation response and initial success to choose repeat therapeutic endoscopy.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Moderate/hard predicted: chronology, response and stage must all be used.

singleBest.key: Repeat therapeutic upper endoscopy
singleBest.decidingObservation: A genuinely new hemorrhage followed documented initial success, with current circulation restored and a small previously reached target.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Misreading chronology can cause unnecessary rescue or premature bypass of a useful endoscopic stage.

authorGate.deletionTest: Remove the later fresh bleeding and intervention is not established by old stool; remove the resuscitation response and the endoscopy-versus-operation ranking becomes unsafe to assume.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If a properly performed repeat endoscopic treatment failed to control the same bleeding target in the stabilized patient, arterial embolization would become the supported escalation.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Post-answer explanation is restricted to recurrence and the current endoscopic stage; it does not state the next node's keyed rescue.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: The old N2 source hold remains historical. New targeted ESGE verification supports this narrower draft; unresolved shock/large-ulcer ranking remains withheld.

competitorAudit.temptation: Treat recurrence itself as proof that repeat endoscopic rescue has failed.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: The current restored circulation and focal small-ulcer course support the offered endoscopic approach to this new episode. Direct angiographic escalation is not the best offered stage in this record.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Appropriate repeat endoscopic hemostasis is unsuccessful in a patient suitable for angiographic rescue.

competitorAudit.temptation: Anchor on the earlier hypotension and overlook the actual resuscitation response.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: Operative rescue is consequential, but this current record supports an endoscopic recurrence attempt before that escalation.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Less invasive rescue has failed or current physiology/anatomy supports operative control.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: The three labels match the prior stage's procedure category, but the key changes because new failure evidence changes the decision. No statement announces that embolization is available or guarantees its success.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Procedural rescue after unsuccessful repeat endoscopic hemostasis.

reasoning.interpret: Recognize persistent bleeding despite attempted repeat definitive and topical rescue, rather than simply recurrent bleeding after an earlier success.
reasoning.apply: Select an angiographic route instead of repeating the failed access strategy.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Hard predicted: keep recurrence and repeated-control failure distinct despite familiar procedure labels.

singleBest.key: Transcatheter arterial embolization
singleBest.decidingObservation: Actual rescue attempts failed and lavage cannot maintain a targetable view; circulatory support is not escalating.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Further untargeted treatment can delay hemorrhage control or cause injury.

authorGate.deletionTest: Without actual treatment/access failure, the prior node's repeat-endoscopy plan remains defensible. Current support response is retained to avoid an unstable-patient blanket rule.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If lavage instead restored a stable view of an untreated focal vessel and the preceding attempt had ended before targeted therapy, another therapeutic endoscopic intervention could become appropriate.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: The preceding feedback never names this escalation. This explanation stops at embolization and does not name the next node's answer.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: Reuses an existing rescue concept; adds a different actual endoscopic-failure context without moving old FSRS history to a new meaning.

competitorAudit.temptation: Repeat a generally useful modality despite its documented present access/control failure.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: The record describes treatment failure and a persistently untargetable field, not merely a prior procedure or an untreated accessible focus.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: A correctable acquisition/access problem leaves a newly targetable focus for a meaningful repeat intervention.

competitorAudit.temptation: Jump directly from failed endoscopy to operation without considering supported angiographic rescue.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: Operation is a consequential alternative, but the represented maintained circulation and guideline-supported angiographic stage determine the offered ranking in the current record.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Angiographic control is unsuccessful or another current reason requires operation.

options.label: Small mixed meals, fewer simple sugars and drinks between meals

options.label: Three larger low-carbohydrate meals with drinks between meals
options.rationale: Reducing carbohydrate does not address the large nutrient load per meal that contributes to this early post-gastric-surgery response.

after.explanation: The early cramping, palpitations and diarrhea with a normal measured glucose fit an early post-gastric-surgery meal response. authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS

authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Initial dietary treatment before a dietary trial has failed.

reasoning.interpret: The episode's early timing, gastrointestinal/vasomotor features and measured glucose differ from late hypoglycemia or retained-food vomiting.
reasoning.apply: Choose an initial meal-pattern strategy rather than a delayed-emptying diet or carbohydrate restriction with large meals.

singleBest.key: Small mixed meals, fewer simple sugars and drinks between meals
singleBest.decidingObservation: Symptoms follow a large sweet liquid-containing meal promptly, with normal glucose during the spell.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Treating the wrong mechanism can preserve the provoking bolus pattern and prolong symptoms.

authorGate.deletionTest: Without timing and the concurrent glucose, early versus late mechanisms remain uncertain; meal-volume observations distinguish the closest dietary error.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If the dominant evidence were retained solid food and a properly documented emptying delay, a low-fat blended/liquid nutrition plan could become appropriate.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Feedback does not name acarbose or any later medication. The next node requires a new measured late response after actual dietary treatment.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: Diet-component evidence is uneven. No forced meal count, fluid interval or empiric disease probability is authored.

competitorAudit.temptation: Apply a delayed-emptying nutrition strategy to the opposite post-meal physiology.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: That liquid-calorie approach can help a different gastric tolerance problem, but it does not address this early response to a large sweet liquid-containing meal.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Solid-food retention from delayed emptying limits nutrition and appropriate liquid supplements are tolerated.

competitorAudit.temptation: Correct the carbohydrate component while preserving an unfavorable meal-volume pattern.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: Reducing carbohydrate does not address the large nutrient load per meal that contributes to this early post-gastric-surgery response.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Usual meal volumes are tolerated and a separate dietary problem is being managed; this is not the initial dumping strategy.

caseDefinition.learningSummary: The early cramping, palpitations and diarrhea with a normal measured glucose fit an early post-gastric-surgery meal response. Begin dietary changes that reduce bolus size and rapidly absorbed carbohydrate, with liquids taken separately. Normal glucose does not exclude that mechanism. The remaining late episodes include measured hypoglycemia and response to carbohydrate after dietary changes. Consider acarbose for this late post-gastrectomy pattern. Somatostatin-analogue escalation may be appropriate if diet and acarbose are inadequate; this is a preventive plan after the acute episode was corrected.

statementMapping.constructedObservationBasis: Original fictional named patients, dates, drug-exposure histories, acquired findings, operation records and actual response trajectories. Measurements are observations, not new epidemiologic weights, probabilities or clinical cutoffs.
statementMapping.numericRuleBasis: Any patient numbers are constructed observations. Four-hour acquisition and the 14-day BQT course are directly supported protocol/treatment facts, not operational waits.

authorGate.authorVerdict: Draft for independent review; no independent PASS
authorGate.coverTheKey: All options name preventive drugs with parallel timing labels; the task does not say glucose-lowering enzyme inhibitor or identify a mechanism matched only by the key. The acute correction is explicit so emergency carbohydrate treatment is not an omitted competitor.
authorGate.oneStageAndCategory: Preventive pharmacotherapy after acute correction and a completed dietary trial.

reasoning.interpret: The original early symptoms improved, while a later meal-linked episode now has documented hypoglycemia and corrective response.
reasoning.apply: Select the supported medication stage for persistent late dumping rather than a prokinetic or immediate broader escalation.

authorGate.predictedResidentDifficulty: Moderate/hard predicted: distinguish the new residual mechanism and sequence acarbose versus somatostatin treatment.

singleBest.key: Acarbose with meals
singleBest.decidingObservation: Diet was actually tried; the remaining pattern is late hypoglycemia and no medication trial has occurred.
singleBest.consequenceOfError: Treating the former mechanism or skipping the supported targeted stage can leave recurrent neuroglycopenic episodes or add unnecessary treatment burden.

authorGate.deletionTest: Delete the late timing/glucose/correction and the earlier early-response interpretation could persist. Delete actual dietary treatment and a medication-first recommendation is not established.
authorGate.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If adequate diet and acarbose failed or acarbose was not tolerated, octreotide could become a reasonable next medication.
authorGate.fullSequenceCheck: Earlier feedback supplies no medication name or late hypoglycemia rule. This node uses new treatment response and measured late findings, not a repeated early-mechanism question.
authorGate.remainingClinicalLimitation: Selected post-gastrectomy late pattern, not an exclusion of every hypoglycemia cause. Fasting or unexplained episodes would need a separate evaluation.

competitorAudit.temptation: Escalate directly to a broader injectable treatment when a targeted oral step remains.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: Somatostatin analogues are an escalation option, particularly after dietary measures and acarbose have not controlled symptoms. No acarbose trial has yet occurred in this record.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: Adequate dietary measures and acarbose fail or cannot be used and a clinician selects further pharmacologic escalation.

competitorAudit.temptation: Treat any post-gastric-surgery meal symptom with a familiar gastric-motility medicine.
competitorAudit.whyNotHere: A prokinetic addresses delayed gastric emptying, not the represented late hypoglycemic consequence of rapid post-gastric-surgery nutrient delivery.
competitorAudit.reasonableWhen: An adequately established delayed-emptying disorder requires a suitable prokinetic and contraindications are absent.

rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treat post-cure IgG or use empiric resistance-prone salvage.

rankedConcepts.testingRelevanceReason: Major gap in this topic and practical operative judgment; low-certainty operative recommendations disclosed.

rankedConcepts.title: Gastric nutrition and route-specific response

rankedConcepts.title: Post-gastrectomy early and late meal responses

rankedConcepts.consequence: Persistent episodes or inappropriate treatment escalation.

reviewRecords.title: Hypergastrinemia during PPI therapy after Billroth II
clarityIssues: "Obtain supervised gastrin/acid assessment" does not identify the actual testing or medication-management plan. It is less concrete than the named investigations in the other options.

cues.phrase: but its specimen map is absent
cues.why: A named missing record points directly to the only option that begins "Review reconstruction anatomy".

cues.phrase: Review reconstruction anatomy and obtain supervised gastrin/acid assessment
cues.why: The key is the uniquely broad, cautious assessment plan against two specific testing strategies; its flexibility shields it from the constraints applied to the alternatives.

fairness: The elevated gastrin with pH 6 during PPI treatment does not establish inappropriate acid hypersecretion. Recognizing confounding and choosing safe reassessment rather than immediate localization are two consequential steps.

The intended key is the best general direction, but its unspecified content prevents a precise comparison with secretin testing. No confident clinical inaccuracy is established from the displayed text; exact testing conditions require clinician confirmation.

Standalone case and task are coherent. All judgments in this report are offline editorial judgments from candidate fields and preceding candidate explanations, not fresh source verification or clinical approval. High-yield and difficulty ratings are qualitative.
suggestions: Name a concrete specialist-led diagnostic plan and its relevant testing conditions at the same specificity as the competing plans; do not invent a withdrawal protocol.

Replace the named omission with meaningful available operative/pathology observations if reconstruction interpretation is to earn a separate inference. Retain active-ulcer safety and the actual pH/PPI observations.

reviewRecords.title: Reassessing H. pylori after discordant post-treatment tests

cues.phrase: while she was still taking omeprazole
cues.why: The only option explicitly correcting this exposure is "Urea breath testing after PPI washout"; a reader can match the medication problem to the uniquely qualified option.

cues.phrase: Repeat serum H. pylori IgG testing
cues.why: Two choices say "Repeat" a test or procedure while only the key supplies a corrective preparation step. This makes the thoughtful/new-plan option visually distinctive.

fairness: Prepared active-infection testing is the best offered plan. Positive IgG cannot settle persistence, and an on-PPI negative stool test is not an adequate cure assessment. The absence of alarm features makes repeat invasive evaluation less compelling.

Interpreting discordant tests and selecting an appropriate reassessment is a worthwhile two-step objective. The numeric preparation statements in feedback were not independently source-verified in this offline review.
The next node follows coherently after a positive prepared breath test; this explanation does not name the subsequent eradication regimen.
suggestions: Make preparation scope comparable across options, preferably in shared context where clinically appropriate, so only the key is not furnished with an explicit corrective qualifier.
Keep competing investigations concrete and clinically plausible. Retain the prior medication exposure rather than hiding the information necessary to judge the negative result.

reviewRecords.title: Salvage eradication after a clarithromycin course
clarityIssues: "The prepared urea breath test" is sufficient after the preceding node, but does not independently state the actual preparation when this node is read on its own.

cues.phrase: She has never received bismuth quadruple therapy
cues.why: Names the treatment family appearing only in the key, immediately before the regimen-selection task.

cues.phrase: The prior clarithromycin course was completed
cues.why: Together with the presentation, repeats the already-used drug name and makes repeating that exact regimen an easy elimination.

fairness: Bismuth quadruple therapy is the defensible intended choice after the represented failed clarithromycin regimen when susceptibility results are unavailable. No confident clinical error is identified.

The positive test is already characterized as prepared, and the treatment history directly supplies the familiar salvage branch. This is primarily regimen recall, rather than two substantial inferences.
Chronology and patient identity remain coherent; prior feedback does not reveal the drug combination. Standalone test validity is asserted rather than demonstrated.
suggestions: Compress the repeated prior-course history into a neutral medication record, avoiding advance naming of the unused answer family.

Build a genuine patient-specific regimen choice using verified relevant prior exposure, susceptibility or contraindication information and credible alternatives, or seek explicit acceptance as foundational recall.
For standalone use, provide concise preparation observations sufficient to establish that the positive test represents persistence.

reviewRecords.title: Scheduling eradication testing after a later antibiotic course
fairness: The key is uniquely supported by the stated preparation rule: four elapsed days plus 24 additional days gives four weeks after the most recent antibiotic exposure. The earlier eradication completion date does not govern the later antibiotic effect; the PPI interval is already adequate.

Identifying the relevant exposure and translating its interval into a collection date are consequential steps. Fourteen days is a plausible wrong interval, and immediate collection wrongly ignores the later antibiotic.
Parallel date choices contain no convincing nonmedical cue. This standalone case is clear; clinical washout intervals are not operational laboratory waits.
suggestions: Retain the competing exposure dates and the statement that relevant medicines remain stopped. No editorial revision required; exact clinical intervals remain subject to named clinician approval.

reviewRecords.title: Positive antibody after a valid negative cure test
fairness: The negative stool antigen test has explicit adequate preparation in the displayed record, symptoms have resolved, and later IgG positivity does not itself establish persistent infection. No additional eradication course is the best offered answer.

The resident must validate the earlier active test, weigh it against serology, and apply that interpretation to prescribing. Both treatment distractors embody the credible error of treating persistent antibodies.

The key is the only nonprescribing plan, but that is the actual clinical decision being tested, not an independent wording shortcut. The standalone task is complete and there is no sequence dependency.
suggestions: No editorial revision required. Preserve the preparation details; removing them would turn this into unsupported dismissal of a potentially invalid negative test.

reviewRecords.title: Incomplete gastric-emptying acquisition

cues.phrase: A solid-meal emptying study
cues.why: Only the key repeats the named study family: "Solid-meal scintigraphy with four-hour acquisition".

cues.phrase: with no narrowing or obstructing lesion
cues.why: The completed adequate endoscopy directly disposes of repeat pyloric inspection; esophageal manometry has no supplied esophageal symptom target. The alternatives leave little meaningful competition.

fairness: A standardized later acquisition is a defensible next investigation after the described limited study; no confident clinical error is identified. The normal two-hour report must not be treated as a normal complete protocol.

As offered, this is essentially recognition of the missing acquisition duration followed by selecting the only gastric-emptying test. The exclusion of obstruction is necessary, but does not by itself create a second consequential step.
The subsequent delayed four-hour result follows coherently and does not leak backward into this question.
suggestions: Retain the actual acquisition log and adequate outlet examination. Compare credible investigations or protocol corrections at the same decision stage, with observations that distinguish them.
Do not merely add more symptoms or obscure the duration. If a fair competing decision cannot be built, seek explicit basic-item acceptance.

reviewRecords.title: Diet after documented delayed gastric emptying

cues.phrase: retains smooth soups and blended meals
cues.why: Repeats "blended" in the key and announces the tolerated texture before the choice.

cues.phrase: large raw-vegetable meals and added bran
cues.why: The failed diet directly matches "added bran supplements" in a distractor; the remaining high-fat solid-food option also opposes the stated solid-food tolerance.

fairness: The low-fat, low-fiber small-meal plan is clinically defensible. The main problem is discrimination, not a demonstrated inaccuracy.
Delayed emptying is already supplied, and the exact tolerated texture is supplied. Matching the prescribed diet to that texture is a single uncomplicated application.

The sequence from adequate testing to dietary treatment is coherent. Read alone, the node supplies delayed emptying, but does not repeat the earlier exclusion of structural obstruction; its context is strongest with the preceding node.
suggestions: Make competing nutrition plans plausible for the same patient and avoid a unique tolerated-texture word match.
Use a verified consequential nutrition tradeoff or actual response discrepancy, rather than simply offering the failed diet again. Preserve necessary diagnostic context for standalone display.

reviewRecords.title: Long-term nutrition after a successful jejunal trial

cues.phrase: During a nasojejunal trial, the prescribed feed was delivered and retained
cues.why: Names the successful route and directly matches "Jejunal enteral feeding access".

cues.phrase: Gastric tube feeds caused repeated regurgitation
cues.why: Explicitly defeats the gastric option; the only successful trial is also the only unused long-term enteral answer.

fairness: Jejunal access is the best offered route given actual successful postpyloric delivery after oral and gastric failure. Parenteral nutrition is not equally compelling in this represented course.
The facts make the answer fair but almost entirely explicit. Converting a successful temporary route into access for the same route is not two consequential inferences.
The later admission and escalation follow coherently from the oral-diet node and stand alone because route failures and trial success are restated. Earlier feedback does not reveal jejunal access.
suggestions: Retain the successful-trial evidence rather than concealing it to manufacture difficulty. Recast around a genuine remaining access or support decision with plausible competitors and patient-specific observations.
If the educational objective remains simply enteral-before-parenteral selection after a successful trial, request explicit foundational acceptance rather than claim resident-level difficulty.

reviewRecords.title: Reassessing a confounded gastric-emptying result
fairness: The technically complete duration does not remove opioid and glycemic confounding. Interval symptom improvement makes persistent motility dysfunction uncertain before an invasive pyloric decision; repeating a prepared functional study is the best offered investigation.

The two consequential steps are judging the validity of the prior abnormal result and choosing what uncertainty to resolve before intervention. Pyloric distensibility is a credible temptation, but does not establish whether the original delay persists.

No option-length, convergence or diagnosis-label shortcut independently identifies the key. The standalone story is coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; specific preparation protocols are not defined or verified here.
suggestions: Optional feedback cleanup: replace "a universal drug-hold or glucose cutoff invented for the case" with learner-facing advice to use the relevant validated preparation protocol. Keep the medication record and interval response.

reviewRecords.title: Prokinetic selection after a metoclopramide movement reaction
fairness: The raw neck and eye findings support a prior acute dystonic reaction, making metoclopramide re-exposure inappropriate. Among the offered medicines, erythromycin addresses gastric emptying whereas ondansetron addresses nausea rather than emptying.

Recognizing the adverse reaction and then choosing an alternative for the specified physiologic target are two consequential steps. The three oral drug labels are parallel; the causal history is necessary medical evidence, not a nonmedical word match to the key.

The standalone presentation supplies documented gastroparesis and failure of dietary therapy. No confident clinical error is identified; this does not establish a long-term erythromycin regimen or eliminate every prescribing safety consideration.
suggestions: No required editorial revision. Feedback could briefly explain the limited durability of erythromycin benefit if supported by the approved claim set; avoid implying indefinite treatment.

reviewRecords.title: Current ulcer stigma versus prior bleeding history

cues.phrase: No hemostatic intervention was performed
cues.why: Directly conflicts with the distractor label "during monitored post-hemostasis care". A reader can reject that option from event wording without interpreting the ulcer stigma.

cues.phrase: High-dose pantoprazole during monitored post-hemostasis care
cues.why: The qualifier gives this option a different care setting and stage, whereas both other options are ordinary oral prescriptions.

fairness: A flat pigmented mark with a stable course supports oral ulcer-healing PPI treatment rather than a new high-risk post-hemostasis course. The historical clipped ulcer does not determine the present lesion risk.
Classifying current stigmata and applying the classification despite prior history is a useful two-step objective, but the option-stage cue bypasses its central distinction.

The record-review frame is coherent and standalone. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. Famotidine is a less effective ulcer-treatment alternative, not inherently an impossible medication.
suggestions: Compare acid-suppression regimens at the same stated decision time without attaching "post-hemostasis" only to the high-dose distractor.
Preserve the flat-versus-protruding observation and chronology; they should determine the regimen, rather than a label for an intervention already stated not to have occurred.

reviewRecords.title: Selecting the ulcer site for endoscopic hemostasis
clarityIssues: "A rounded red projection" is less precise than a clearly described vessel morphology. The intended nonbleeding visible vessel is inferable, but the wording could prompt uncertainty about an adherent clot; this is a realism/description concern, not a confident claim that the key is wrong.

cues.phrase: a rounded red projection persisted above the ulcer floor
cues.why: This is the single visibly exceptional site against two flat/even floors. It directs attention to the keyed site, although knowing that it merits hemostasis still requires medical knowledge.

fairness: The intended duodenal-bulb visible-vessel target warrants hemostasis despite a dry field; the flat pigmented and clean-base gastric sites do not create equally persuasive targets.

All three options name the same intervention at different sites and are grammatically parallel. However, recognition of the one high-risk stigma almost entirely resolves the question; multiple sites do not create a second consequential decision.
The standalone site map is internally consistent. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified from the intended morphology.
suggestions: Clarify the actual vascular appearance using a clinician-checked description or usable original exhibit without adding the interpreted risk label.

Add a genuinely consequential management distinction with credible alternative actions after stigma interpretation, or obtain explicit basic-recognition acceptance. Do not inflate difficulty with additional decorative sites.

reviewRecords.title: Continuing early PPI therapy despite a later dry view
clarityIssues: The reason for the repeat EGD is absent; it could imply routine second-look endoscopy is expected despite no new bleeding. The test can be a supplied historical event, but its role should be clear.

cues.phrase: only one day of the initial post-hemostasis PPI course had been completed
cues.why: "Only" and an explicitly incomplete "initial" course point to continuing that course rather than making the learner determine the treatment phase.

cues.phrase: Continue the initial high-dose pantoprazole course
cues.why: Repeats "initial" and "course" from the update, while both alternatives begin "Change". The continuation wording reinforces the incomplete-course cue.

fairness: The intended plan is defensible: successful treatment of initial spurting does not become a low-risk initial lesion merely because a subsequent view is dry. The explanation appropriately avoids insisting on continuous infusion as the sole high-dose route.
Interpreting the later endoscopic finding in light of the index stigma and elapsed treatment time can support two steps. The current phrasing supplies too much of the phase interpretation.
Standalone chronology is otherwise coherent. The exact duration in feedback was not freshly source-verified in this offline review; no confident clinical error is identified.
suggestions: State neutral elapsed time and actual treatment received rather than "only" and "initial ... course ... completed". Use parallel continue/change or regimen labels across options.

Remove the unexplained routine-repeat impression by providing a clinically credible reason for the documented second view, or use a relevant interval observation that genuinely affects the comparison. Keep the index bleeding stigma.

reviewRecords.title: Recurrent ulcer bleeding after initially successful endoscopy
fairness: The later hematemesis, hemoglobin fall and transient hypotension establish a materially different event from the earlier isolated dark stool. Current restored blood pressure and pulse, successful initial control and an accessible focal lesion support repeat therapeutic endoscopy as the best offered procedure.

The resident must distinguish residual evidence of prior bleeding from recurrence and then choose the appropriate rescue stage. Embolization and surgery are credible downstream alternatives, not nonsensical procedures.

All options are concrete hemostatic procedures of comparable scope. No decisive nonmedical cue was found. The first node is complete on its own; its explanation names the current decision without revealing the next node's embolization answer.
suggestions: No editorial revision required. Preserve the distinction between the two bleeding observations and the actual post-resuscitation measurements.

reviewRecords.title: Escalation after repeat endoscopic hemostasis fails
clarityIssues: "Blood pressure was maintained without increasing support" does not give the achieved pressure or identify the support already required. Maintained severe hypotension and maintained adequate perfusion are materially different records.

"Topical rescue briefly obscured it" could describe loss of visibility rather than a transient hemostatic response. Continued fresh blood establishes failure, but the intended sequence would be clearer with the actual observation.

cues.phrase: Repeated lavage could not maintain a targetable view
cues.why: Directly makes "Another therapeutic upper endoscopy" unattractive. This is necessary treatment-feasibility information, but reduces the effective comparison to embolization versus surgery.

fairness: Failure of the repeat therapeutic attempt makes embolization a reasonable intended next step. Interpreting persistent bleeding rather than temporary obscuration and applying the rescue sequence are consequential.

The current physiologic summary is insufficiently concrete to fully assess the closest competitor, operative hemostasis. This is an unresolved ranking concern, not a confident assertion that surgery is equally best in the intended stable patient.

The sequence follows the recurrent-bleeding node without a premature answer leak. Read alone, this node gives repeat-treatment failure but lacks the earlier lesion details and actual resuscitation measurements; do not silently borrow an earlier blood pressure as a current one.
suggestions: Give concise actual contemporaneous blood pressure/perfusion and support trajectory observations that establish the intended resuscitation state, without inventing a treatment threshold.
For independent display, include the necessary same-ulcer site/size and prior-treatment context within this node or its visible presentation.
Describe what topical therapy did to bleeding and visualization directly, preserving uncertainty if the source of obscuration cannot be determined.

reviewRecords.title: Operative rescue after unsuccessful embolization

cues.phrase: a collateral that the microcatheter could not enter
cues.why: Directly defeats "Repeat selective catheter embolization" as written.

cues.phrase: The endoscopic field remained obscured
cues.why: Directly defeats "Repeat therapeutic upper endoscopy"; surgery is the only option not expressly made infeasible.

fairness: Continued extravasation and hematemesis with rising support needs after unsuccessful endoscopic and angiographic rescue make operative hemostasis the best offered direction. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.
The actual raw observations are important and should remain. However, both alternatives are expressly defeated, so general elimination selects surgery without two consequential medical inferences.

The three-part rescue chronology is coherent, and the preceding explanations do not explicitly give away surgery.
